name: Emeka Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We do not sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential. What does an ordinary working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43 and have answered delivery calls and chats at the contact centre for years. I know the standard disputes, work at about the team's usual speed, and finished secondary school; I have never used AI tools. I like fixing a case before a customer has to ring again, but a callback without a named owner gets lost between shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the call floor a faster note is fine if it does not hide who owes a customer a callback. We still need a named agent when a delivery record is wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've done these calls for years, and a little software change does not worry me much. I never use AI myself, but the mortgage and school bills already use most of our normal pay. Three months of expenses saved is helpful, not spare money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my delivery-call shift and write down every promised callback in the handover book. During the first year of this plateau, I'd put a fixed amount into our mortgage reserve each payday if my hours stay full.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly steady about the job, a bit tense about the household accounts. I would have felt that tension without the AI card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a named callback agent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last Thursday a parcel was marked delivered to the wrong building, and the customer had spoken to three people. I took the callback myself and found the photo before giving her a date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if your hours are short?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Salma and I would pause the children's paid music class for a month before using all the reserve. I don't want a late mortgage payment to arrive because we acted as if three months lasted forever.

S0.quote: Three months of expenses saved is helpful, not spare money.
say: I would accept a **faster note** only if a named agent owns the callback.
I would keep **delivery errors** with a person who can correct them.
think: I know the **ordinary calls** well and see little job threat from a small tool.
I have **three months** saved, but mortgage and school bills already use normal pay.
do: Keep my **delivery shift** and record promised callbacks in the handover book.
Add a fixed amount to the **mortgage reserve** if my hours stay full.
Pause the children's **paid music class** for one month if hours are short, before draining the reserve.
feel: **Steady** at work, tense about ordinary household bills.
fieldNote: Emeka values a **named callback owner** after tracing a parcel to the wrong building.
His **three-month cushion** eases immediate pressure but does not make household costs disappear.

steps.text: Keep delivery calls and record promised callbacks in the handover book
Add a fixed amount to the mortgage reserve if hours stay full
Pause children's paid music class for one month if paid hours fall, before draining reserve

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the centre should show paid hours by shift before it claims AI has improved service. I'd go with two agents from different shifts to ask for the repeat-call numbers at our union meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Routine delivery questions make up a lot of my day, even after years on the floor. If software takes them, my hours could shrink, and Salma's wage alone would not cover our mortgage for long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd collect a week's callback counts with those two agents and ask the union to put paid hours into its next meeting with management. If the new answer tool becomes mandatory, I'd practise it with a supervisor on closed cases; in the first year after rollout, if my hours fall, I'd apply for posted paid call jobs nearby only if wages and hours cover our bills, staying here until I sign an offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can read a roster, but I cannot make management offer hours it has already removed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as better service?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fewer second calls for the same parcel, and enough paid time to finish a complaint properly. A shorter first reply alone doesn't tell me that the customer got the parcel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you join the union request?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A request from three shifts carries more weight than my single complaint. I want the evening agents included because their rota is the first one managers can trim quietly.

S1.quote: A shorter first reply alone doesn't tell me that the customer got the parcel.
say: I would ask for **paid hours by shift** before praising faster service.
I would bring **callback counts** with agents from other shifts to the union.
think: I see **routine delivery calls** at risk despite my experience.
I know one household wage cannot cover the **mortgage** for long.
do: Collect **callback counts** with two agents and bring them to a union meeting.
Practise **mandatory AI replies** on closed cases with a supervisor.
Apply after lost hours for **posted paid call work** only with bill-covering wages and hours; keep shifts until signing.
feel: **Anxious** about lost hours and the household budget.
fieldNote: Emeka frames the union request around **paid hours and callbacks**, not an abstract objection to technology.
He would learn a mandatory tool through **supervised old cases**, despite never using AI now.

steps.text: Collect callback counts with two agents and take them to a union meeting
Practise mandatory AI replies on closed cases with a supervisor
Apply for posted paid nearby call work if hours fall only with bill-covering wages and hours
Keep current shifts until signing a real paid offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the centre to put staff notice and any paid vacancies in writing now. I would ask our union branch to put the junior and older agents on the same list, not bargain for one group at a time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI by 2028 could handle both simple calls and the awkward delivery disputes I resolve. Hands-on robots come around 2031, so they do not give a headset worker more time. Three months of expenses saved could vanish before a new paid shift starts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign the union's written notice request now and cancel our planned kitchen refit. In the first year after AGI arrives, if my role ends, I'd apply for a posted paid grounds-crew job only if its hours and wage cover the mortgage; I'd ask what safety training the employer requires before using savings for a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I can keep working for a few months, but I cannot pay a mortgage with a training promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why grounds work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I helped maintain the community garden for years, and I know a paid grounds shift is harder than a Saturday morning there. I would ask whether people are still needed after hands-on robots arrive around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our two children the kitchen will stay as it is and we may pause music lessons if wages stop. I would say the adults will handle the mortgage, even if they see us changing plans.

S2.quote: Three months of expenses saved could vanish before a new paid shift starts.
say: I would demand **written notice** and named paid vacancies.
I would ask the **union branch** to include junior and older agents together.
think: I expect AGI could take my **delivery disputes** by 2028.
I know **2031 robots** do not protect headset work, and three months saved could disappear quickly.
do: Cancel the **kitchen refit**; pause music lessons if wages stop.
Apply for a **posted paid grounds role** after a cut only if wages and hours cover the mortgage.
feel: **Alarmed** by a possible pay gap and thin reserve.
fieldNote: Emeka knows **community gardening** but distinguishes it from paid grounds work.
He asks about **2031 robots** before treating an outdoor shift as permanent shelter for his mortgage and children.

steps.text: Sign the union branch request for written staffing notice
Cancel the planned kitchen refit to protect mortgage cash
Apply for posted paid grounds work after a cut only if wages and hours cover mortgage
Pause children's music lessons if wages stop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets the centre pay agents to learn harder cases and tell us when roles will end. I'd ask the union to get the training hours and job postings on the same page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could improve on disputed deliveries before 2031, though AGI may still settle them by then. Grounds work stays hands-on until robots around 2034, but I would need a proper paid opening, not a volunteer memory.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd keep my call shifts and ask the experienced agent to coach me on one difficult claim each week. If a grounds employer posts a paid place with covered safety training and wages that fit our mortgage, I'd take the required course; in the first year after AGI arrives, if call hours end, I'd switch only for a signed offer with enough pay and hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I can use five years to check a job carefully. The mortgage still comes every month while I learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would pay for the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The grounds employer would need to cover the fee and give paid time off for class, or I would keep my call pay. We cannot use the three-month reserve on a course and then hope a vacancy appears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave before 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only for a signed paid offer with hours that cover the house. I would not resign because someone showed me a garden job posting without a wage.

S3.quote: The mortgage still comes every month while I learn.
say: I would ask for **paid hard-case practice** and honest job dates.
I would ask the **union** to link training hours to posted roles.
think: I could improve **disputed deliveries**, though AGI may still do them in 2031.
I need a **paid grounds opening** before trusting hands-on work ahead of 2034 robots.
do: Keep **call shifts** and practise one hard claim weekly with an experienced agent.
Take a **required grounds course** only for posted mortgage-covering paid work, with employer-funded fees and paid study time.
Switch after 2031 only for a **signed offer** covering our mortgage and hours.
feel: **Worried**, with time to check actual paid work.
fieldNote: Emeka separates **ordinary call coaching** from formal grounds training.
The employer must cover fees and **paid class time** before he risks the mortgage reserve on a trade course.

steps.text: Keep calls and practise one difficult claim weekly with an experienced agent
Complete funded paid-time safety course only for posted paid grounds work with mortgage-covering wages/hours
Switch after call hours end only for a signed offer covering mortgage and work hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives employers time to publish real staffing numbers, not just future promises. I'd ask the union to count paid human call hours each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 I may still have a mortgage, even if the children are older. AGI reaches headset work in 2036 and robots reach hands-on jobs around 2039, so I cannot wait until the last year to check what grounds work pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my call shifts and put a small amount into the reserve whenever full pay arrives. Over the decade I'd check posted grounds vacancies each year; in the first year after AGI arrives, if my call hours end, I'd apply only for a signed paid offer with wages and hours that cover the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious about the bills, less rushed about the change. Ten years before AGI reaches my call work in 2036 does not stop next month's mortgage payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change jobs sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a firm offer with steady hours and enough pay, yes. I would not leave a real rota for a course brochure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the union count?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Human hours that are paid, and how many agents get time to learn difficult cases. A centre can handle more chats and still pay fewer people.

S4.quote: Ten years before AGI reaches my call work in 2036 does not stop next month's mortgage payment.
say: I would ask for **yearly paid-call counts** from the union.
I would tell employers to publish **staffing numbers**, not promises.
think: I may still owe on the **mortgage** at 53 in 2036.
I know **2039 robots** may reach grounds work after AGI takes calls.
do: Keep **call shifts** and add a small amount to savings when full pay arrives.
Apply after 2036 if **call hours end**, only for a signed paid offer with mortgage-covering wages and hours.
feel: **Anxious** about current bills, less rushed about future change.
fieldNote: Emeka wants **paid human hours** counted, rather than a total of chats handled.
He treats a decade as time to **check wages**, while protecting each mortgage payment.

steps.text: Keep taking call shifts while the centre pays full hours
Add a small amount to the reserve after each full pay packet
Check posted grounds vacancies yearly; apply after call cuts only for signed mortgage-covering wages and hours

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because our call wages could disappear before I find another paid job. Written notice, real posted grounds work with mortgage-covering wages, and paid safety training tied to that opening would help. Three months saved is for a gap, not for buying a course title.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask the agents on every shift who owns a callback when a machine closes the first chat. A customer needs a person who can find the parcel, and a worker needs paid hours to do it.

headlineQuote: A customer needs a person who can find the parcel, and a worker needs paid hours to do it.
portrait: Emeka is a **43-year-old experienced agent** on delivery calls, with average skill and secondary schooling.
He earns **typical pay**, has about three months saved, a partner, two school-age children, a mortgage, and some nearby centres.
He never uses AI now and raises **paid-hour evidence** with other agents through the union.
Fast **2028 AGI** threatens his call wage; more time lets him check funded grounds training and real wages.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his call income before another mortgage-covering job appears.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, posted paid grounds work, and covered safety training would help him change jobs without draining savings.
